files.content:
/**
 * The field anatomy, shared by every control that wears it — `TextField`,
 * `SearchField`, and the textarea, select, checkbox and radio still to come.
 *
 * The styling lives here, and so does the one piece of field *state* React Aria
 * leaves to us: the validation context `Slider` — the one field it does not treat
 * as a field — publishes for its own `Error` slot. See
 * `FieldValidationContext` at the bottom of this file.
 *
 * Each component defines its own slot components, thin as they are, so that its
 * docs and manifest describe its own API rather than pointing at another
 * component's.
 */
import { createContext } from 'react'

/**
 * The three control sizes. `size` is set once on the field and travels as two
 * custom properties rather than through React context: the control, and any
 * affix inside it, are ordinary descendants of the field, so inheritance already
 * does the work. It also means a one-off override is just a utility on the
 * element rather than a new prop.
 */
export type FieldSize = 'sm' | 'md' | 'lg'

export const FIELD_SIZES: Record<FieldSize, string> = {
  sm: '[--field-control-h:2.25rem] [--field-control-text:0.8125rem]', // 36px / 13px
  md: '[--field-control-h:2.75rem] [--field-control-text:0.875rem]', // 44px / 14px
  lg: '[--field-control-h:3.25rem] [--field-control-text:0.9375rem]', // 52px / 15px
}

/**
 * The sheet's `.ds-field`: legend, control, then the hint that explains it.
 *
 * The `font-size` here is what the control and any affix inherit. It sits on the
 * field rather than on the input so it still reaches an affix, which is the
 * input's sibling — a `cap`-sized icon would otherwise match the page's font
 * instead of the field's.
 *
 * The two border properties are published here for the same reason `Checkbox`
 * publishes its own: read-only lives on the field root, while the border it changes
 * is on the input, and a group variant cannot win that cascade — see the note on
 * `INPUT`. Declaring them here means the input only reads them, and the ordinary
 * cascade decides, because `[data-readonly]` plainly outranks the bare declaration.
 */
export const FIELD = [
  'group flex flex-col gap-2 [font-size:var(--field-control-text)]',
  '[--field-border:var(--color-input)]',
  '[--field-hover:var(--color-border)]',
  // Read-only is not disabled: the value is the whole point of the field, so it
  // keeps full-strength text. Only the affordances go — a quieter hairline, and no
  // brightening on hover — because there is nothing here to invite a click on.
  'data-[readonly]:[--field-border:var(--color-border-soft)]',
  'data-[readonly]:[--field-hover:var(--color-border-soft)]',
].join(' ')

/**
 * The sheet's `.ds-affix` wrapper. `Group` exists for one case: an affix is
 * positioned against the control, but the field also holds the legend and the
 * hint, so an affix anchored to the field would centre on all three.
 * Wrapping the control gives the affix the right box — and it stays opt-in, so a
 * plain field has no extra element at all.
 *
 * The two `:has()` rules are here for the same reason: the room an affix needs is
 * padding on the input, and the group is what can see both of them. The input
 * itself never has to know it has neighbours.
 */
export const GROUP = [
  'relative flex w-full',
  'has-[[data-slot=icon-start]]:[&>[data-slot=input]]:ps-10.5', // 42px, per the sheet's search field
  'has-[[data-slot=icon-end]]:[&>[data-slot=input]]:pe-14', // 56px, per the sheet's trailing unit
].join(' ')

/**
 * The sheet's `.ds-field-legend`: 12px, uppercase, letterspaced, white 70%.
 *
 * The required marker is drawn from the field's own `data-required`, so the label
 * never has to be told and the asterisk cannot drift out of sync with
 * `isRequired`. The input already carries the native `required`, so this is the
 * visual half of the same fact.
 */
export const LABEL = [
  'text-[12px] uppercase tracking-[0.04em] text-muted-foreground',
  "group-data-[required]:after:ms-1 group-data-[required]:after:text-destructive group-data-[required]:after:content-['*']",
].join(' ')

/**
 * The sheet's `.ds-input`.
 *
 * The resting hairline is what identifies the control. The sheet gives
 * `.ds-input` a transparent border and leaves the panel-2 fill to do the job, but
 * that fill is 1.23:1 on the dark page and 1.17:1 on the light one, so the field is
 * nearly invisible as a boundary in both. `--input` is the smallest
 * hairline that clears the 3:1 a control boundary needs on each.
 *
 * Hover has to *strengthen* it rather than replace it: the sheet's hover is white
 * at 25%, which is now weaker than the resting line and would erase it.
 *
 * `outline-none` on focus suppresses the *browser's* ring, which is what the
 * sheet's `.ds-input:focus { outline: none }` is really doing. Chrome gives a
 * focused text input its `:focus-visible` ring at `outline-style: auto` regardless
 * of React Aria's attribute, so leaving it alone means a blue UA ring on a teal
 * system. Focus is then the border alone — adding the shared 3px-offset ring here
 * would draw two parallel teal hairlines with a gap, which reads as a fault.
 * `Button` can carry that ring because the edge it repeats is a solid fill.
 */
export const INPUT = [
  // **The corner is a token now, and `rounded-md` is the control step of its scale.** Pulse's own
  // `--radius` is `0`, so the sheet's square field is unchanged here; a theme that sets a radius
  // moves every control in the library at once. See the radius note in `docs/theming.md`.
  'w-full font-mono rounded-md border border-(--field-border)',
  'h-(--field-control-h) px-3.5',
  'bg-muted text-foreground placeholder:text-foreground/35',
  'transition-[border-color,background-color] duration-(--duration-fast) ease-pulse',
  // Focus and invalid stay literal, so they outrank the published border and always
  // win — including on a read-only field, which is still focusable and still the
  // field the caret should be able to reach.
  'data-[hovered]:not-data-[focused]:border-(--field-hover)',
  'data-[focused]:outline-none data-[focused]:border-primary',
  'data-[invalid]:not-data-[focused]:border-destructive',
  // The browser already knows when someone has left a field invalid, so the state needs no
  // "touched" class and no blur listener — it only needed a rule. Same line in `TextArea`.
  'user-invalid:not-data-[focused]:border-destructive',
  'data-[disabled]:cursor-not-allowed data-[disabled]:opacity-40',
  // Read-only gets the cursor and nothing else that dims it. `opacity` here would
  // take the *value* down with it — at 40% the text measures 3.42:1, under the 4.5:1
  // body text needs, so the one thing the user came to read becomes the thing they
  // cannot.
  'group-data-[readonly]:cursor-not-allowed',
].join(' ')

/** The sheet's `.ds-hint`: 12px, tighter tracking, white 55%. */
export const HINT = 'text-[12px] tracking-[-0.5px] text-foreground/55'

/**
 * The sheet paints its error state yellow, because the original design had only
 * two accents and yellow was the nearest thing to a warning it owned. That does
 * not carry over here: `--warning` is this system's `secondary` button, so
 * errors would be the same colour as a secondary action. The error state uses
 * `--destructive`, the danger hue, and keeps the sheet's flex so an icon can be
 * dropped in front of the message.
 */
export const ERROR =
  'flex items-center gap-1.5 text-[12px] tracking-[-0.5px] text-destructive'

/**
 * The sheet's `.ds-affix__unit` and `.ds-affix__icon`: pinned to the control's
 * box, vertically centred, and never a click target — the affix is decoration, and
 * a pointer-events-owning overlay would swallow clicks meant for the field. Sized
 * in `cap` like `Button.Icon`, so one icon works at every field `size`.
 */
export const ICON = [
  'absolute inset-y-0 z-10 grid place-items-center pointer-events-none',
  'text-foreground/70',
  '[&>svg]:block [&>svg]:h-[1.5cap] [&>svg]:w-auto [&>svg]:shrink-0',
].join(' ')

/** The sheet insets both affixes 14px from their edge. */
export const ICON_POSITIONS = {
  start: 'start-3.5',
  end: 'end-3.5',
} as const

export type IconPosition = keyof typeof ICON_POSITIONS

/**
 * The invalid state of a control React Aria does not treat as a field, published by that control
 * itself.
 *
 * **Every other field here reads its invalid state from React Aria.** `TextField`, `Select`,
 * `Switch` and the rest are handed `isInvalid`, and React Aria publishes the
 * `FieldErrorContext` their `Error` slot renders from. `Slider` is left out of that anatomy:
 * `useSlider` takes no `isInvalid` at all, and a slider *thumb*'s is deprecated with no
 * replacement — which is why this component's docs never showed a `FieldError`. (`TokenField` is
 * left out for the same reason and stays out: its message can be neither rendered nor reached. See
 * docs/components/tokenfield.md.)
 *
 * So `Slider` publishes the context itself, from an `isInvalid` prop the caller owns. That is
 * exactly what an integration binding a slider to a form has: a value it validated and a failure it
 * has to report. What it is *not* is React Aria's form validation — the `validationErrors` a
 * `Form` carries are keyed by field name and read by React Aria's own fields, and a slider never
 * sees them.
 *
 * **`errorId` is minted by the control, not by the slot**, because the message and the element it
 * describes are two different slots and only the control can own the name they share.
 */
export const FieldValidationContext = createContext<FieldValidation | null>(
  null,
)

export interface FieldValidation {
  /** Whether the control's value is invalid. */
  isInvalid: boolean
  /** The id the control's error message wears, so the control is described by the message. */
  errorId: string
}

/**
 * The `ValidityState` of a field nothing is wrong with — React Aria's own shape for "there is no
 * native input to ask", which is the situation for a slider.
 *
 * It is never read: `FieldError` looks only at `isInvalid` and `validationErrors`, and the
 * rest travels to a render-function child that never asks. It is here because React Aria types the
 * context as a `ValidationResult`, and a field that claims to be valid should carry a valid
 * object rather than a cast.
 */
export const VALID: ValidityState = {
  badInput: false,
  customError: false,
  patternMismatch: false,
  rangeOverflow: false,
  rangeUnderflow: false,
  stepMismatch: false,
  tooLong: false,
  tooShort: false,
  typeMismatch: false,
  valid: true,
  valueMissing: false,
}

/**
 * The sheet's `.ds-select-menu`, shared by everything that opens over the page: `Menu` now, and
 * `Select` and `ComboBox` when they converge onto it. The same split as `field.ts` — the surface is
 * the thing that must not drift, and the slots are still defined per component so Storybook
 * documents them under the right name.
 *
 * The shadow is the one literal colour in this file: it is a **shadow**, not a surface, and every
 * attempt to derive one from a token produces a haze rather than a shadow. It is `rgba(0,0,0,.7)`
 * because a shadow has to darken in both themes, exactly as the modal's scrim does.
 */
export const SURFACE = [
  'border border-border-strong bg-card rounded-xl',
  'shadow-[0_12px_32px_rgba(0,0,0,.7)]',
  // **A transparent outline at rest, never `outline-none`.** The property is shared —
  // `outline-none` writes `--tw-outline-style`, which every `outline-<width>` reads
  // back — so a ring written beside it can never draw. `Popover` is the part here that
  // takes real focus (a popover with no focusable child is focusable itself).
  'outline-1 -outline-offset-2 outline-transparent',
].join(' ')

/**
 * A popover that holds a single scrolling list: **at least as wide as the control it came from, and
 * wider when an option needs it.**
 *
 * `min-w`, not `w`. A trigger is sized for its own label — a `Select` says "Frankfurt", a `Menu` button
 * says "Actions" — and a panel sized to exactly that cuts off the one option longer than the control,
 * which is usually the option the reader opened the menu to find. Growing to fit the content is what a
 * native popup does, and `w-(--trigger-width)` was the only rule here that could not.
 *
 * The `max-w` is the guard that growth needs: it is the window minus the same 1rem gutter the modal's
 * overlay keeps, so a label long enough to run off the page truncates instead. `min-width` outranks
 * `max-width` in CSS, so a trigger already wider than that cap (a full-width field on a phone) still
 * gets its own width and is never squashed. React Aria writes `--trigger-width` as an inline custom
 * property and no width of its own, so this class is what decides.
 */
export const POPOVER = `flex min-w-(--trigger-width) max-w-[calc(100vw-2rem)] flex-col overflow-clip ${SURFACE}`

/** The list inside it. `max-h` so a long list scrolls rather than running off the page. */
export const LIST =
  'max-h-[264px] overflow-auto overscroll-contain p-0 outline-none'

/**
 * The sheet's `.ds-select-option`: 13px at 75%, with the accent reserved for the choice.
 *
 * Hover and focus land on the same treatment on purpose. A menu is walked with the arrow keys as
 * much as with a pointer, so the row the keyboard has reached and the row the pointer is over
 * should not look like two different kinds of thing.
 */
export const ITEM = [
  'relative flex items-center justify-between gap-3',
  'px-3.5 py-[11px] text-[13px] text-foreground/75',
  'cursor-pointer select-none',
  'data-[hovered]:bg-foreground/7 data-[hovered]:text-foreground',
  'data-[pressed]:bg-foreground/12',
  'data-[focus-visible]:outline-none data-[focus-visible]:bg-foreground/7 data-[focus-visible]:text-foreground',
  'data-[selected]:text-primary',
  'data-[disabled]:cursor-not-allowed data-[disabled]:text-foreground/35',
].join(' ')

/** One item's text, which truncates rather than wrapping a menu wider than its trigger. */
export const ITEM_LABEL = 'truncate'

/** A run of items, announced as a group. */
export const SECTION = 'flex flex-col'

/** The sheet's `.ds-select-group-label`. */
export const SECTION_TITLE = [
  'px-3.5 pt-[9px] pb-1',
  'text-[11px] uppercase tracking-[0.08em] text-foreground/45',
].join(' ')

/** The sheet's `.ds-div-hair`, inset so it reads as a break in the list rather than a table edge. */
export const SEPARATOR = 'my-1 h-px shrink-0 bg-border'

/** A search box above the list sits behind the menu's own hairline, so it reads as part of the surface. */
export const SEARCH = 'border-b border-border-strong p-2'

/**
 * A submenu's caret. A row with a submenu says so — `data-has-submenu` is React Aria's — and an
 * affordance nobody can see is not an affordance.
 */
export const SUBMENU_CARET = [
  'shrink-0 text-foreground/45',
  'motion-safe:transition-[rotate] motion-safe:duration-(--duration-fast) ease-pulse',
  'data-[open]:rotate-90',
].join(' ')

docs:
A time, typed or chosen — `TimeField` with a picker attached.

```tsx
<TimePicker defaultValue={parseTime('09:30')} minuteStep={15}>
  <TimePicker.Label>Opens at</TimePicker.Label>
  <TimePicker.Group>
    <TimePicker.Input />
    <TimePicker.Button />
  </TimePicker.Group>
  <TimePicker.Hint>Business hours only.</TimePicker.Hint>
</TimePicker>
```

| Slot                | React Aria   | Notes                                      |
| ------------------- | ------------ | ------------------------------------------ |
| `TimePicker`        | `TimeField`  | Owns the value. `size` is `sm \| md \| lg` |
| `TimePicker.Label`  | `Label`      | The shared field legend                    |
| `TimePicker.Group`  | `Group`      | Leaves room for the chevron                |
| `TimePicker.Input`  | `DateInput`  | The segments, drawn from the render props  |
| `TimePicker.Button` | `Button`     | The chevron that opens the wheel           |
| `TimePicker.Hint`   | `Text`       | `slot="description"`                       |
| `TimePicker.Error`  | `FieldError` | Renders nothing while valid                |

### The wheel is drawn for you, and it stays open

A picker without a wheel is not a picker, so `TimePicker` renders the popover and the three columns
itself, and the field is the entire API — as in `DatePicker`, the popover and its contents are
internal and cannot be replaced.

**Picking does not close it, and that is the one place this differs from `DatePicker`.** A day is one
decision, so choosing one closes the calendar. A time is two, three or four — hour, minute, and then
seconds or a day period if the field has them — and closing after the hour would send the reader back to
the field to start again. Enter and Escape close it; Escape is React Aria's own, and Enter is captured
before the option under the keyboard can consume it, because by then the option has nothing left to do:
the value was committed when the arrows moved focus onto it.

### It is `TimeField`, not a second time field

`TimePicker` wraps React Aria's `TimeField`, so the segments, the label, the hint, the error and the
validation are the field's — the same ones `TimeField` publishes, through the same `field.ts` and
`date.tsx` recipes. What the picker adds is the trigger, the panel and the wheel; what it does not add
is a second way to type a time.

The value is a `TimeValue`, not a string. `parseTime('09:30')` reads an ISO time and `onChange` hands
back the same shape, which is what keeps the segments, the order they appear in and the wheel's own
numbering following the locale rather than a format the code chose.

### Every column follows a segment

**The wheel offers exactly what the field shows, and that is a rule rather than a coincidence.** A
`TimePicker` built with `granularity="second"` has a second segment, so its wheel has a seconds column;
a minute field has neither and gets neither; a 24-hour locale has no day period to name, so there is no
AM/PM column. Offering seconds to a field that cannot show them writes a value nobody can read back, and
hiding them from a field that has them throws away the precision it was built for.

That is why the seconds column appears from `granularity` and not from a prop of its own: the segments
are the field's own answer, read from the `TimeFieldState` React Aria publishes, which is the same state
that draws them. `secondStep` then decides how far apart the seconds in that column are — one by default,
so every second the field can hold — and `minuteStep` does the same for the minutes.

### The wheel asks the field what its hour cycle is

**Nothing here decides between 12-hour and 24-hour time.** The hour column is built from the hour
segment's own `minValue`/`maxValue`, and the day-period column exists only when the field's segments
contain a `dayPeriod` — both read from the `TimeFieldState` React Aria publishes, which is the same
state that draws the segments. An `en-US` clock gets twelve hours and an AM/PM column; `en-GB` gets
twenty-four and none; a locale whose hour runs `0–11` gets that. A second, independent decision about
the hour cycle is how a wheel ends up offering 12 next to a field that has no such segment.

The AM/PM labels come from the same formatter the field uses, so a `ja-JP` field reads `午前` in the
segment and in the wheel. Hardcoded `AM`/`PM` would put the two halves of one component at odds.

### What the columns had to decide

| State                        | Treatment                                |
| ---------------------------- | ---------------------------------------- |
| out of `minValue`/`maxValue` | dimmed to 30%, and skipped by the arrows |
| chosen                       | filled with the accent, carrying `ink`   |
| hovered / focused            | the sheet's faint wash                   |

Out-of-range times stay in the column rather than being removed — a column with holes in it is harder
to read than one where the gaps are marked. A **whole hour** is only dimmed when every minute in it is
outside the window: with `minValue` at `09:30`, hour 09 is offered because 09:59 is inside it, and a
column that dropped the hour a reader is living in would be unusable. Choosing it then **clamps** —
09:00 lands on 09:30 — so arrow-scrubbing across a boundary stays inside the window instead of asking
the field to reject its own value.

The hover and focus washes are qualified with `not-data-[selected]` so a chosen time keeps the accent
under the pointer and under the keyboard. Written without it, the two rules set the same property at the
same specificity, and which one wins is the order Tailwind emits them in — a coin toss the source
cannot show you.

### The behaviour is React Aria's, not a re-implementation

Each column is a React Aria `ListBox`, and the wheel's whole keyboard story is that choice:

- **`selectionBehavior="replace"` commits as focus moves**, so `ArrowDown` changes the value with no
  Space to confirm — the reason a wheel beats typing into segments.
- **`autoFocus` lands on the value that is set**, not on the first row, because React Aria's autofocus
  prefers a selected key. It also scrolls that option into view.
- **`disabledKeys` keeps the arrows off everything outside `minValue`/`maxValue`**, and typeahead
  (`45` in the minutes column) comes free with the collection.
- **Left and right move between the columns**, landing on the value each one holds so the next arrow
  steps from what is set — and the seconds column is part of that walk, not an afterthought beside it.
  The direction follows the locale: in RTL, `ArrowLeft` moves forward. Tab also moves between them,
  because React Aria treats each list as one tab stop.

The wheel is a row of columns rather than a clock face for the same reason: a list box can be read,
typed into and walked with the arrow keys, and its options carry `data-selected` and `data-disabled` for
the eye. There are three of them for a minute field and four when the field holds seconds — which is also
why a seconds wheel is wider than the field it belongs to, and the popover grows to fit the wheel rather
than the trigger.

### Four things this cost, all worth writing down

- **A bare `Time` cannot be committed.** React Aria types `setValue` for a date field and takes every
  plain value through `toCalendar`, which asks the value for its calendar — and `@internationalized/date`'s
  `Time` deliberately has none, so `timeState.setValue(new Time(9, 30))` throws. The wheel commits a
  `CalendarDateTime` carrying the field's own date, and `useTimeFieldState` maps what it emits back
  through `toTime`, so `onChange` still receives a `Time`.
- **`timeValue` is declared non-nullable and is `null` while the field is empty**, because React Stately
  computes it from the value. An empty field opens the wheel on its **placeholder** rather than on a
  time this component picked — the same midnight the segments are showing, or whatever `placeholderValue`
  says. That is why `placeholderValue` is published here and not on `TimeField`.
- **`minValue`, `maxValue` and `placeholderValue` are not on the state.** React Aria consumes all three
  when it builds `TimeFieldState` and does not publish them again, so they travel to the wheel through
  this component's own context rather than being read back off the state.
- **React Aria scrolls the column it focuses, and only that one.** The hours column is autofocused when
  the wheel opens, so it arrives on the value that is set — and a seconds column of sixty opened at `00`
  with the second it was set to somewhere below the fold, which looks exactly like a column that ignored
  the value. The wheel now scrolls every column to its own selected row, on the render _after_ the
  collection exists (React Aria builds it a commit late, which is why its own autofocus retries), and
  again whenever what the wheel is showing changes — but not while a reader is scrolling a column they
  are browsing, because browsing changes no value.

### Form behaviour is the field's

A `TimePicker` carries exactly the form plumbing a `TimeField` has, because it _is_ one — native
constraint validation through `validationBehavior`, the `FieldError` slot, `validate`, and React Aria's
hidden input. It does not add a hidden input of its own, and that is deliberate: React Aria sets the
hidden input's `form` attribute to `''` (`react-aria-components/src/HiddenDateInput.tsx`) so a time
field's value is not submitted with a form. A second, submittable input here would make `TimePicker` and
`TimeField` disagree about the same value.

### The trigger is disabled with the field

React Aria's own `DatePicker` leaves its chevron enabled on a disabled field, and the input dims alone.
Here the trigger dims and disables with it: a picker that cannot be edited must not open a panel that
would write to it. Read-only is not an exception — there is nothing to invite a click on.
